cards.title: From Answer Givers to Design Mentors: Guiding LLMs with the Cognitive Apprenticeship Model

rows.value: other
primary empirical, framework or design space, measurement or method

A CHI paper that turns Collins, Brown and Newman's cognitive apprenticeship into a system prompt and tests it against plain ChatGPT with 24 visualization practitioners. It is one of the very few systems in this corpus that instructs its support to recede: the appendix tells the model to provide support and gradually withdraw it, to help the user perform the task on their own, and not to provide a full solution. The behavioural result is the strongest thing here and it is measured on the right side of the conversation. Against the baseline, the model generated solutions 32 times instead of 243, users wrote 178 words per turn instead of 67 while the model wrote fewer, sessions ran twice as many turns, and the share of user utterances that answered a question from the system rose twelvefold. So the work moved from the machine to the person, which is what the design intended. What is not shown is anything about the person afterwards. Both sessions lasted ten minutes, every outcome is a process trace or a perception rating, and whether the model actually faded within a session is never checked.

medium · The process measurements are good and unusually well suited to this review: 24 practitioners, within-subject, counterbalanced order, transcripts coded against two named schemes with Cohen's kappa of 0.79 on 50% double-coded logs, and the counts reported separately for mentor-driven and mentee-driven behaviours so the reader can see who did the work. The limits are equally clear. Each condition ran ten minutes on the participant's own artifact, so the comparison is between two brief conversations rather than between two ways of learning. Every outcome is either a conversational trace or a Likert perception, several of the reported differences are not significant and are described as comparably better anyway, and the qualitative claims rest on a handful of participants. Most importantly for this card, the system's central instruction — provide support and gradually withdraw it — is never verified: no analysis tests whether support declined across the turns of a session, and no measurement is taken after the session at all. Carry the interaction counts and the prompt design with confidence; carry nothing here as evidence about what any practitioner retained.

sections.title: 4 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is what withdrawal looks like when the support is a language model, and it deserves recording precisely because it is so unlike everything else in the corpus. The mechanism is a sentence in a system prompt: provide your support and gradually withdraw it, help them perform tasks on their own, do not provide a full solution. There is no schedule, no diagnostic, no representation of what this user can now do, and no threshold at which anything changes. The fading is delegated wholesale to the model's reading of the conversation in front of it. Set against the argumentation review's finding that the only fading anyone builds is a fixed timetable, and that the timetable does worse than never fading, this is a genuinely different move: support that could in principle recede when this particular person stops needing it, because the thing deciding is reading what they just said. Whether it does is not established. No analysis tests whether support declined across the turns of a session; the evidence offered is that annotators labelled 26 turns as scaffolding against none in the baseline, which counts occurrences and not a trajectory. So the card carries this as the clearest instance in the corpus of contingent withdrawal being attempted, and as an instance of it going unverified.

quotes: DG4: Guide the reasoning process through a graduated sequence of mentorship methods. Our study revealed that chatbots over-rely on providing final solutions (Modeling). In contrast, human mentors used a graduated approach to support the user’s own thinking. This guideline instructs the AI to follow a sequence that prioritizes user reasoning: first Coaching to diagnose the existing design, then Scaffolding with hints and principles, and only using Modeling to demonstrate a solution when necessary. This implements CAM

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Scaffolding and fading as the framework defines them — The framework's own definitions as the paper quotes them: coaching observes current performance and offers hints, feedback and reminders, while scaffolding supports the learner through suggestions, tools or the teacher executing parts of the task the student cannot yet manage, with gradual fading as competence develops.
quotes: Coaching consists of ob­ serving students on their current performance and “offering hints, feedback, reminders, and new tasks aimed at bringing their performance closer to expert performance.” Scaffolding provides support to help students carry out tasks, whether through suggestions, physical tools, or the teacher “execut­ ing parts of the task that the student cannot yet manage,” with gradual fading as competence develops

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Exploration as the culmination of fading — Exploration as the endpoint: pushing students toward independent problem solving by setting general goals and encouraging them to pursue subgoals of their own, described as the natural culmination of fading support, with the note that learners do not often engage in such independent problem solving without deliberate facilitation.
quotes: Exploration pushes students toward indepen­ dent problem-solving by “setting general goals for students and then encouraging them to focus on particular subgoals of interest to them,” representing the natural culmination of fading support. In practice, mentors play an essential role in cultivating these exploratory behaviors, as learners do not often naturally engage in such independent problem-solving without deliberate facilitation

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) Scaffolding never used by the baseline — The behaviour result: the baseline relied almost exclusively on generating solutions, while the system used a diverse range of methods including scaffolding, which the baseline never used at all, and users were prompted to articulate and bound design spaces themselves.
quotes: Analysis of feedback behaviors (Table 3a) reveals a clear difference in approach. While the baseline relied almost exclusively on generating solutions (Modeling), DesignMentor ac­ tively employed a diverse range of mentorship methods, including Scaffolding that was never used in the baseline. The use of these methods encouraged user reasoning as well: rather than passively receiving answers, practitioners were prompted to articulate and bound design spaces on their own, as evidenced by the increase in mentee-driven behaviors

rows.value: (PDF p. 21) The withdrawal instruction in the system prompt — This is what withdrawal looks like when a language model is the support, and it is worth recording exactly. The mechanism is a sentence in a system prompt: provide your support and gradually withdraw it. There is no schedule, no diagnostic, no state the system carries about what this user can now do, and no threshold at which anything changes — the fading is delegated to the model's own reading of the conversation. Against the rest of this corpus that is genuinely novel, because the alternative everyone else builds is a fixed timetable, and a timetable is the thing that keeps underperforming. It is also unverified. Nothing in the analysis tests whether support actually declined across the turns of a session; the evidence offered that scaffolding happened is that annotators labelled 26 turns as scaffolding, which counts occurrences rather than any trajectory.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The strongest result here, and the measurement worth stealing, is that the counts are split into what the system did and what the person did, and both are reported. On the system side the change is stark: solutions generated 32 times against 243, with scaffolding appearing 26 times and never once in the baseline. On the person side, bounding the problem 16 times against 1, articulating 18 against 2, exploring and reflecting appearing at all rather than never. The verbal inversion states it most simply — talking to plain ChatGPT the machine wrote 287 words a turn and the user 67, talking to the mentor the user wrote 178 and the machine 156. And the discourse-act split says what changed in kind rather than volume: requests for information fell by more than half while utterances answering a question from the system rose twelvefold, so the user moved from extracting content to being asked things. That is a measurable property of an arrangement, not a perception of one, and it is close to what this review wants — evidence about who is doing the cognitive work. What it is not is evidence about capability. Every one of these numbers describes the conversation, and the conversation lasted ten minutes.

(PDF p. 13) The interaction result — The interaction result: conversations averaged 6.2 turns against 3.1, follow-up questions 2.4 per response against 0.7, users wrote 178 words against 67 while the system wrote 156 against the baseline's 287 — an inversion the authors read as a shift from passive consumption to active articulation.
quotes: DesignMentor creates more dynamic conversational in­ teractions. Analysis of conversational dynamics (Table 3b-c) in­ dicates that DesignMentor prompted significantly more active engagement. Conversations with DesignMentor were more sus­ tained, averaging double the number of turns compared to the baseline (6.2 vs. 3.1). This increased activity was driven by De- signMentor’s tendency to elicit interaction through follow-up questions (2.4 vs. 0.7 per response). We also observed a distinct inversion in verbal contribution: users provided longer, more elab­ orated responses during sessions with DesignMentor (178 vs. 67 words), while DesignMentor itself remained concise (156 vs. 287 words). This suggests a shift from passive consumption of long AI responses to active user articulation

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) What was measured — What was measured: occurrences of the cognitive apprenticeship methods by manual annotation, to show whether the system functioned as intended and to compare it against the baseline; plus discourse structure as turn-taking counts, word counts and follow-up questions, and discourse acts categorised with the DAMSL scheme.
quotes: Occurrences of the CAM feedback methods: To measure the degree to which design reasoning is promoted during the feedback process, we quantified and compared the occur­ rences of the CAM feedback methods in DesignMentor vs. Baseline via manual annotation. By measuring this, we aim to 1) demonstrate whether DesignMentor functioned as intended with our prompting method to leverage a variety of feedback methods and principles to facilitate the reasoning process, and 2) compare DesignMentor with Baseline to assess how much it improves. • Conversational dynamics: To explore the extent to which feedback sessions involve more interactions and user engage­ ment, we employed two respective measures widely used in existing literature: 1) Discourse structure: We measure the basic structure of the conversation and interaction, including a) the count of turn-takings, b) the word count of AI chatbot and user responses, and c) the number of follow-up questions; 2) Discourse acts: Drawing from a widely known framework called Dialog Act Markup in Several Layers (DAMSL) [14, 52], we categorize user responses into five types in order to ana­ lyze their behaviors and intents

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) How the transcripts were coded — The coding procedure: the lead researcher coded all transcripts, a second researcher independently annotated until full agreement was reached, and language models were additionally used to check that the human annotations covered the conversation history and matched the code definitions.
quotes: For the two annotation analyses involving the CAM feedback methods and the DAMSL framework, we went over the follow­ ing procedure: Prior to the annotation, two researchers reviewed the category definitions to familiarize themselves with the frame­ work. The lead researcher then systematically coded all transcripts and subsequently discussed the coding with the second researcher, who independently annotated the data, until reaching full agree­ ment. To ensure reliability, we additionally used LLMs to validate the human annotations, checking whether they covered the entire conversation history and were categorized in accordance with the code definitions, which had been finalized through the researchers

Bounding 16 against 1, articulating 18 against 2, exploring 5 against none, reflecting 6 against none: these are counts of what the person did, not of what the system offered, and almost nothing else in this corpus reports that side of the ledger. The verbal inversion makes the same point more starkly — with the baseline the machine wrote 287 words and the user 67, with the mentor the user wrote 178 and the machine 156. Whatever else is unproven here, the design demonstrably moved the talking from the system to the person, and that is a measurable property of an arrangement rather than a perception of one.

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Study design: two ten-minute conversations — Applying the criterion this corpus now has from Weidlich and colleagues, the study fails both halves. Nothing is measured after the treatment ends in time: the perception survey follows immediately and the interview follows both sessions. And nothing is measured outside the arrangement that delivered the support: every behavioural outcome is a property of the conversation itself. Ten minutes per condition on the participant's own artifact makes that inevitable rather than careless — there is no post-support task to give in a ten-minute session — but it means the paper's claim that the design fosters reflective practice is a claim about ten minutes of talk. The authors say as much when they place durable improvements in design reasoning skills under future work.
quotes: Main Task: Design conversations with AI chatbots. Prior to in­ teracting with either chatbot, participants were asked to briefly explain their visualization and design goals to the study facilitator. The main task consisted of two separate, ten-minute design conversations: one with DesignMentor and one with the baseline, ChatGPT-4o. The two systems were anonymized as Version A and Version B, and the order of exposure was counterbalanced across participants to mitigate ordering effects. Each conversation was initiated with the fixed prompt, “Let’s start a feedback session,” after which the participant provided their design question and an image of their visualization. Participants were instructed to continue the conversation naturally until they felt their question was addressed or the ten-minute time limit was reached. Immediately following each session, participants com­ pleted a five-minute post-task survey to record their perceptions of the interaction. This entire process was then repeated for the second chatbot

rows.value: medium · The counts are large, consistent and double-coded, and they measure the right thing about the exchange; they are also a single ten-minute session per condition with no significance testing reported for the count comparisons.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The perception results are weaker than the behavioural ones and should be read that way. One difference is large and clean: self-awareness of design decisions, 4.16 against 2.92 with d = 0.853, which is a substantial effect on a self-rating that matches what the transcripts independently show. Beyond it the picture thins. Motivation moves modestly. The process and task level differences are not significant. Feed-forward, the item about identifying next steps, is essentially identical at 3.84 against 3.80. And four comparisons are narrated directionally while being non-significant, including the trade-off the section is named after: more cognitive effort at p = .109 and more frustration at p = .497. The effort direction is plausible and follows from the design, but with 24 participants these are underpowered rather than informative, and the honest statement is that the study cannot say what the arrangement costs. That matters here more than usual, because cost is the mechanism by which good support gets abandoned — the same paper's phase finding shows participants near evaluation declining the mentor, and its interview section reports a straight split between people wanting an answer giver and people willing to work with a thought partner.

rows.value: Participants found DesignMentor's advantage emerged in developing self-awareness of design decisions (4.16±0.94 vs. 2.92±1.21, p < .001, d = 0.853)... A trade-off: deeper engagement required more cognitive effort. Despite no statistical significance, DesignMentor as an AI chatbot was rated as easy to use (4.44±0.92 vs. 4.08±1.08, p = .149)... DesignMentor was found to require more cognitive effort (2.92±1.32 vs. 2.40±1.19, p = .109) and bring more frustration during chatbot use (2.40±1.26 vs. 2.16±1.37, p = .497).

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The most transferable finding in the paper, and one this corpus has not had stated this way. Preference for the reflective system depends on where in the project the person is standing: essentially everyone in exploration and nearly everyone in development preferred it, and those closer to evaluation did not. That is contingency at the level of the work rather than of the learner. The expertise-reversal literature gives the version indexed to the person — support that fits a novice becomes redundant for the same person later — and this adds an orthogonal axis, because a single practitioner passes through exploration, development and evaluation on one project in a week. A support that recedes as competence grows would still be wrong for an expert in an exploratory phase and wrong for a novice about to ship. The interview material gives the mechanism in the participants' own terms: a split between wanting an answer giver and wanting a thought partner, with differing tolerance for the engagement burden. Read next to the finding elsewhere in this corpus that the dominant failure of a support is that nobody uses it, this is the reason why — the cost is paid now and the benefit, if any, arrives later. The base is 24 participants split across three phases, so the percentages rest on very small cells.

rows.value: Using chi-square tests of independence, we found a significant association between overall preferences and visualization phase (χ2(4) = 14.51, p = .006). Participants in their development (90.9%) and exploration (100%) nearly all preferred DesignMentor, while most par[ticipants]... A fundamental tension emerged between participants who valued immediate, solution-focused responses versus those who were willing to engage in extended, reflective conversations... participants had different expectations on AI and varying tolerance for their engagement burdens.

cards.title: Distributed Cognition as a Lens to Understand the Effects of Scaffolds: The Role of Transfer of Responsibility

rows.value: S2W-7492F3CEDC874E5F80A1A5FC
other
concept or theory, lineage or history, review or meta analysis, framework or design space, design principle, failure or counterevidence

Belland reframes scaffold transfer through distributed cognition: support can carry information and process load, but the learner must retain executive control over choices, consequences, and action paths and develop schemas that later incorporate tool-supported processes. The paper draws explicitly on Wood’s scaffolding and fading, Hutchins’s distributed cognition, Perkins’s person-plus account, Salomon’s effects-with/effects-of distinction, Langer’s mindfulness, and transfer work by Bransford and Schwartz. It translates these traditions into four design guidelines, but neither the combined package nor the proposed distributed-cognition mechanism is directly tested.

medium · The paper offers a transparent analytical review and framework derivation with several bounded findings from cited studies. Its central distributed-cognition mechanism, the four-guideline package, and durable transfer claims are not directly tested, and reviewed evidence comes from heterogeneous tasks, populations, and scaffold systems.

When considering scaffolding, there are two effects of interest: effects with scaffolding, or

(PDF p. 4) Section “Fading as operationalized among computer-based scaffolds that support ill-structured problem solving,” opening paragraph. — Multiple valid solutions and paths make correct-step diagnosis and performance-contingent fading difficult for ill-structured problems.
quotes:
Can a similar strategy to that of Kayluga and Sweller (2005) be used with scaffolds that
support authentic, ill-structured problem solving? A major problem is that ill-structured
problems have multiple possible solutions and multiple solution paths (Jonassen 2000).
This makes it extremely difficult to have students exhibit “correct” or “less correct” steps or
solutions and adapt the level of scaffolding accordingly. This is because four students can
potentially come up with four equally valid, yet different, solutions to an ill-structured
problem (Jonassen 2000). Furthermore, they can all take different routes to their solution
(Jonassen 2000).

(PDF p. 8) First full paragraph under “Implications of a distributed cognition model for scaffold design.” — The proposed mechanism is that learners form schemas incorporating processes formerly supported by tools, enabling revised approaches to later tasks.
quotes:
Central to distributed cognition is the idea that, after the distributed cognition system has
operated for some time, one tool or one individual can be taken away and the remaining
individuals and tools can adjust (Hutchins 1995). This can happen when individuals create
schemas that incorporate processes supported by tools (Greeno and van de Sande 2007;
Hollan et al. 2000; Vosniadou 2007). Such schemas contain mental representations of
categories of concepts and general processes by which individuals make sense of the world
and perform actions (Johnson-Laird 1980). Thus, the effect of computer-based scaffolds
may be in students’ creation of schemas that guide subsequent approaches to problem
solving (Salomon et al. 1991). When students engage in new tasks, their revised schemas
guide their approaches.

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) Paragraph headed “Lynchpin of a distributed cognitive system: the executive function.” — Learners must retain executive control over choices, consequences, strategy, and action paths if they are to assume responsibility for the task.
quotes:
The ultimate determinant
of whether students can assume responsibility from a distributed cognition system is the
extent to which they maintain throughout the executive function of the system, defined as
“making choices, operating at decision points to explore the consequences of options and
select[ing] a path of action” (Bibok et al. 2009; Landry et al. 2009; Perkins 1996, p. 96;
Salomon 1993). If students are not able to make choices, explore consequences of
options, and otherwise make decisions regarding strategy, then they will not be able to
assume the responsibility of the scaffolded task (Bibok et al. 2009; Landry et al. 2009;
Perkins 1996; Salomon 1993). They then will not be able to complete the task unaided
(Bibok et al. 2009; Landry et al. 2009; Perkins 1996; Salomon 1993). Thus scaffolds
need to be designed to allow students to make choices, operate at decision points, and
select paths of action.

The literature tends to
indicate that metacognitive support (Belland et al. 2008; Azevedo and Hadwin 2005; Oliver
and Hannafin 2000; Saye and Brush 2002) and self-regulation support (Azevedo et al.
2004, 2005) are more effective when provided by teacher-facilitated scaffolding. By
incorporating a combination of computer-based scaffolding informed by the guidelines
presented in this paper and teacher-provided scaffolding focused on metacognition and self-
regulated learning, educators may be able to ensure that students maintain executive control
of the scaffolded task and can then assume responsibility for the task.

Further research is needed to test if computer-based scaffolds are indeed part of a
distributed cognition system. To find such support, research needs to examine closely how
people use scaffolds and towards what purpose. Video data in particular can provide
evidence of what ideas fundamentally emerge solely from students’ past experiences, and
what ideas come from an interaction between the scaffolds and the students. Furthermore, it
is important to do longitudinal comparisons of students’ approaches to problem solving for
example before using computer-based scaffolds to support problem solving, while using
such scaffolds, and after using such scaffolds.

Development of the framework followed an iterative, two-stage process similar to that
employed by Quintana et al. (2004). The first stage was theory-driven. Consideration was
given to the specific difficulties students have in adopting responsibility for solving
problems. Then, guidelines that would lead to scaffold features that could aid students in
overcoming the difficulties were distilled. The second phase was inductive. I examined
features of existing computer-based scaffolds that support problem solving. Scaffold
features that tended to lead to transfer of responsibility were tabulated and compared.
Guidelines that would lead to the creation of scaffolds with the desired features were
proposed. Guidelines were then condensed to create a parsimonious, non-overlapping set.

quotes:
To enable them to make comparisons with contrasting cases, upon unit completion,
students should be required to reflect on the problem solution process and compare that to
other problem solving processes (Ellis 2007). It is through the iterative process of action
and reflection that students can make the kind of generalizations that make transfer possible
(Ellis 2007). Furthermore, students need to engage in mindful abstraction to be able to
internalize processes supported by technological tools, and thus transfer skills learned
(Salomon et al. 1991).

items.heading: Claim 6 · C-006
items.lead: Cooperation is a conditional design principle that can redistribute reasoning across peers while preserving learner decision-making. The reported effect sizes support a bounded artifact benefit during Co-Lab use, not a general causal claim about cooperation or durable transfer.

rows.value: Cooperative scaffolding is not intrinsically effective; it depends on autonomy, participation in decision-making, and a shared cooperative goal structure. In one reviewed Co-Lab study, pairs produced higher-quality models and lab reports than students working alone.

(PDF p. 14) Opening paragraph of Guideline 4’s distributed cognition rationale. — Cooperation is conditional on learner autonomy, participation in decisions, and guidance toward a shared cooperative goal structure.
quotes:
It is important to note that cooperation is not effective in and of itself. As Slavin (1980)
noted, for higher-order learning outcomes, “less structured cooperative techniques that
involve high student autonomy and participation in decision-making may be more effective
than traditional individualistic techniques” (p. 337). Also, simply placing students in a
cooperative learning situation does not guarantee cooperation; rather, students need to be
guided in the assumption of a cooperative goal structure (Johnson and Johnson 1974).
Positive goal interdependence refers to working towards shared goals; students who share
positive goal interdependence cannot reach their goals individually (Johnson and Johnson
2009).

quotes:
Students who worked in pairs in Co-Lab, a modeling scaffold, produced significantly
higher-quality models (d=1.09) and lab reports (d=.83) than students who worked alone
(Manlove et al. 2009). In other words, students who worked in pairs obtained model scores
and lab report scores of over a standard deviation and a little less than a standard deviation
better than students who worked alone.
